title: Having Everything and Enjoying Nothing
summary: The Teacher describes a man to whom God gives riches, wealth, and honor, yet who is not allowed to enjoy them, and he judges that a stillborn child is better off. Appetite is never satisfied, the wise have no final advantage over the fool, and no one can contend with the one stronger than he. The chapter ends with two questions no human can answer: what is good for a person in a fleeting life, and what will come after him.
story: Chapter 5 closed on a hopeful note: God gives wealth and the power to enjoy it, and that is a gift. Chapter 6 turns the coin over. What if God gives the wealth but not the enjoyment? The Teacher sets the two cases side by side on purpose, because the difference between them is not something a person can secure by effort. It lies in God's hand. This short chapter also works as a hinge in the book. Its closing questions, about what is good and about what comes after, gather up the first half of the Teacher's search and set the agenda for the second half, where chapter 7 immediately begins a series of sayings about what is better.
historical: The chapter contains no datable event, but it speaks to a society in which wealth, a large family, long life, and an honorable burial were the recognized marks of a blessed life. In the ancient Near East, to have a hundred children and live many years was a proverbial picture of success, the kind of life credited to patriarchs and kings. The Teacher takes that ideal and pulls the ground out from under it. Whether the book comes from Solomon's time or, as many scholars hold, from the Persian or early Greek period, its readers knew a world where fortunes could pass suddenly to strangers through war, debt, confiscation by rulers, or the lack of an heir, the situation verse 2 describes.
cultural:
Burial mattered enormously in the ancient world. To be denied a proper burial was a disgrace and, in the view of many peoples, a lasting misery; the prophets threatened the wicked with lying unburied (Jeremiah 22:18-19). That is why the Teacher mentions it in verse 3: a man might have every outward blessing and still die unmourned and unhonored. The stillborn child, by contrast, never saw the sun, never had a name that anyone remembered, and yet has more rest than the man who lived two thousand years without enjoying good. The comparison is meant to shock. Job made the same wish in his agony (Job 3:11-16), and the Teacher uses it here as a measure of how empty prosperity without enjoyment is.

The idea that naming something shows authority over it runs through the Old Testament. God names the day and night in Genesis 1, Adam names the animals in Genesis 2, and kings renamed conquered vassals. So when verse 10 says that whatever exists was named long ago, a first reader would hear a claim about God's sovereign ordering of all things, and the one stronger than man is most naturally God himself.
literary: The chapter has two movements. Verses 1 to 6 are a case study introduced by the Teacher's familiar formula, an evil he has seen under the sun, and built on exaggeration: a hundred children, a thousand years twice over. Verses 7 to 12 are a cluster of short sayings and questions. The Hebrew word nephesh (soul, life, appetite) runs through the chapter: the man lacks nothing his soul desires (verse 2), his soul is not satisfied (verse 3), and his appetite is never filled (verse 7). Verse 9 contrasts what the eye can see with the wandering of desire, literally the going about of the soul. Many readers treat verses 10 to 12 as the midpoint of the book. The key word hevel appears five times, and the questions of verse 12 (who knows, who can tell) prepare for the second half, where the Teacher will show again and again that humans cannot know the future or find out the whole of God's work.

outline.t: God gives wealth but not the power to enjoy it
Better the stillborn than a joyless long life
Appetite never satisfied, and the wandering of desire
What is named, what is foreknown, and who can tell

doctrines.note: Whatever exists was named long ago, and what happens to a man is foreknown (6:10). God has ordered the world before anyone enters it, and no person can contend with him. The Teacher does not explain why God gives some the power to enjoy their goods and withholds it from others; he simply refuses to pretend that this lies within human control.

Human beings are creatures of appetite whose desire always outruns what they have (6:7, 9). The Teacher's observation fits the wider biblical picture of people made for God, whose longings cannot be filled by the goods of the world alone.

The chapter names a kind of suffering that has no outward sign: a life full of blessings that brings no joy. Scripture does not dismiss this as ingratitude. It takes it seriously as a grievous affliction (6:2).

words.note: Nephesh, often translated soul, but with a range that includes life, self, throat, and appetite. In verse 7 it is the appetite that is never satisfied, and elsewhere in the chapter it is the desire that lacks nothing yet finds no rest. The word reminds us that in Hebrew thought a person does not have a soul so much as is one: a living, hungry, desiring self.

Hevel, breath or vapor, which appears five times here. The stillborn child comes in hevel (verse 4), the stranger's enjoyment of another's wealth is hevel (verse 2), and life itself is a fleeting life, literally the days of a person's hevel (verse 12). In this chapter the sense of brevity is especially strong: life passes like a breath or a shadow.

Tsel, shadow. Verse 12 says a person passes through life like a shadow. The shadow is a common biblical picture of what is brief and insubstantial (Psalm 144:4; Job 8:9; 1 Chronicles 29:15). It pairs naturally with hevel: both are real, both can be seen, and neither can be held.

christ: Jesus diagnosed the same condition when he asked what it profits a person to gain the whole world and lose his soul (Mark 8:36), using the language of profit that the Teacher uses throughout the book. He told the parable of a rich man whose life was demanded of him before he could enjoy what he had stored up (Luke 12:16-21). And he offered himself as the answer to the restless appetite the Teacher describes: whoever drinks the water he gives will never thirst (John 4:13-14), and he came that his sheep might have life in abundance (John 10:10). The connection is thematic, not predictive. Ecclesiastes names a hunger that no gift under the sun can fill, and the gospel claims that the Giver himself has come to meet it.

hard.q: Is it fair for God to give a person wealth and then not allow him to enjoy it?
hard.a: The Teacher states the problem bluntly in verse 2 and does not solve it. Some readers take this as a mark of his limited, under-the-sun perspective: he reports what life looks like without revealing God's hidden purposes, and the book's larger framework (3:11, 12:14) assures us those purposes exist. Others emphasize that the Teacher is exposing a false assumption, that possessions carry happiness within them. Enjoyment is not a product that comes bundled with wealth; it is a separate gift, and the person who treats goods as the source of joy will be disappointed even when he has them all. A third observation is that the Teacher is honest about experiences many people have, and Scripture includes that honesty rather than hiding it. The chapter does not accuse God of injustice; it shows that the power to enjoy life is not ours to command, which pushes the reader toward humility and dependence.

questions: Have you known someone who seemed to have everything and yet found no joy in it? What does this chapter suggest was missing?
Verse 9 says it is better to enjoy what the eye can see than to be driven by the wandering of desire. What would it look like to practice that this week?
The chapter ends by asking who knows what is good for a person. Where do you look for the answer to that question, and how reliable is that source?
